title: Protocol for glial Ca2+ imaging in C. elegans following chemical, mechanical, or optogenetic stimulation
protocol: Acquire glass needles from borosilicate glass capillaries using a Flaming/Brown micropipette puller.
Procure a 30 cm long soft silicone tubing with about 1 mm inner diameter.
Insert a 200 μL yellow pipette tip at one end of the tube.
Attach a glass needle to the other end of the tube to create a glue pipette.
Carefully break the needle tip at the edge of the square glass to achieve an opening size suitable for the experiment.
Sterilize the yellow pipette tip and place it on the lip to pump GLUture® glue slowly into the pipette.
Pump the glue slowly until it reaches 1/8th of the tip of the needle.
Monitor the needle tip under a microscope constantly during the pumping process to avoid overflow.
Drop 20–40 μL of bath solution in the middle of a 22×22 mm square cover glass.
Transfer one worm gently from an OP50 plate to the bath solution using a worm picker.
If the worm is dirty, relocate it to a clean NGM plate without OP50 bacteria and drop 5–10 μL of bath solution to wash.
Move the cleaned worm back to the square glass for gluing.
Stabilize the worm on the square glass with glue using a glue pipette.
Treat worms gently and smoothly.
Fix the amphid of the worm to the square glass if targeting AMsh glia.
Use a small amount of glue to cement the tail of the worm to avoid movement interference.
Wait for 10 minutes after applying glue.
Mount the square glass to the bottom of the circular chamber with Vaseline.
Place the prepared chamber on the platform of an inverted microscope.
Focus on the target glia labeled with fluorescence protein and genetically encoded calcium indicators like GCaMP5.0.
Use the fluid system (MPS-2 Multichannel Perfusion system) to add odorants and chemicals mixed with bath solution at 0.2 mL/s flow rate.
Keep the pump active all the time to remove bath solution or Isoamyl alcohol (IAA) from the chamber.
Acquire images using CCD camera.
Record glial calcium responses every second using Micro-Manager software for 30 seconds of bath solution application, then 60 seconds of IAA, and finally wash with bath solution for 110 seconds.
Remove the square glass after recording is completed.
Transfer a new worm to the chamber.
Repeat the process with the new worm.
Set the amplifier to give a pulse at a specific time point.
Drop 20–40 μL of bath solution in the middle of the prepared sylgard round coverslip.
Transfer one worm from the NGM plate to the bath solution.
Stabilize one side of the worm with glue, being careful not to submerge the worm's nose.
Wait for 10 minutes.
Insert the coverslip into the square chamber filled with bath solution.
Position the head of the worm toward the touch needle by moving either the coverslip or square chamber.
Place the prepared chamber on the platform of the microscope and focus on the target glia.
Tape the chamber to both sides of the platform to avoid movement.
Operate the objective lens and touch needle side by side carefully; observe the touch needle under the microscope.
Ensure the touch needle tip is very close to the head of the worm but does not touch it before starting the experiment.
Acquire images using a CCD camera.
Start recording using the Micro-Manager software.
Provide mechanical stimuli through the HEKA EPC-10 amplifier and piezoelectric actuator at 20 seconds or 30 seconds.
Move the microscope and touch needle out of the bath solution after completing the experiment.
Repeat the process with a new coverslip.
Use Image-J to analyze the calcium imaging data.
Adhere the CoChR-transgenic worm, which is fed with or without ATR (control), on a square glass using a glue pipette to stabilize the worm.
Wait for 10 minutes.
Place the prepared chamber on the platform of the microscope and focus on the target glia.
Reset the exposure time and interval time to adjust the stimulation frequency.
Set the interval time at 100 ms and the frequency at 5 Hz (460–480 nm).
Ensure the exposure time is not longer than the interval time.
